newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call money rates start to slip.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call money rates start to slip.

text.p: Dutch call money started to slip on Friday after an ample allocation and dealers said it could fall further ahead of next Thursday's first cash reserve expiry under the new money market policy.
Call money rates dropped to 2.68 percent bid after the allocation versus some 2.88 percent on Thursday.
The Dutch central bank allocated 4.07 billion guilders to the money market this morning under a seven-day special advances pact at an unchanged rate of 2.90 percent.
Individual banks' applications were met for 28.8 percent of the amount they had applied for.
"Banks who had applied for liquidity under the pact received a high amount, which probably means there were only a few demanding liquidity," said one dealer.
He added liquidity was unevenly divided.
"Participants who are short of liquidity are catching up now as they receive a fair amount under the current advances pact," the dealer said.
"Others who have sufficient liquidity did not apply for this advances loan," he said, explaining why the allocation could have been sufficient for those who needed it.
The new rules for the money market -- introduced a month ago -- no longer allow banks to show a debit balance at the end of a trading day under the cash reserve facility.
Participants with a debit balance have to borrow money under the marginal advance facility, currently set at 4.5 percent, to move out of debit.
Dealers said several banks had been playing safe and using less liquidity than they could have under the central bank rules.
"This probably means that call money rates can come down further ahead of the cash reserve expiry," said one dealer.
The guilder was a little stronger versus the German mark at 112.49 per 100 marks compared to 112.535 on Thursday.
